lead: Frequency division multiplexing (FDM) sends many messages over one cable, fibre or radio link at the same time by giving each its own band of frequencies. Each message modulates its own carrier, usually as SSB, the bands are placed side by side with small guard bands between them, and the sum is sent as one composite signal. At the receiver, band-pass filters pick each band out and a demodulator brings it back to baseband. Analog telephone trunks carried thousands of calls this way. Radio and TV broadcasting, cable TV and FM stereo are FDM too.
prereq: You need: SSB from SSB and VSB modulation and coherent detection from DSB-SC modulation and coherent detection.

sections.h3: Slots, guard bands and the total bandwidth

blocks.text: Each channel is given a slot of the spectrum. The modulated message fills part of it and the rest is the guard band, an empty strip that lets real filters move from pass to stop without letting a neighbour in. Two ways of counting are in use, and an answer must say which one it uses:
guard bands only between channels: N channels of modulated bandwidth B<sub>ch</sub> each, with N − 1 guard bands of B<sub>g</sub> hertz.
the slot convention of telephone systems: every channel owns a slot of B<sub>ch</sub> + B<sub>g</sub>, with its guard band inside.

With SSB, B<sub>ch</sub> = W; with DSB-SC or AM, B<sub>ch</sub> = 2W. Switching from SSB to DSB doubles B<sub>ch</sub> but not the guard bands, so the total less than doubles: for a 3.1 kHz voice with a 0.9 kHz guard band, the slot is 4 kHz with SSB and 2 × 3.1 + 0.9 = 7.1 kHz with DSB, not 8 kHz.

items: Each message passes a low-pass filter that limits it to W (0.3 to 3.4 kHz for telephone speech).
A balanced modulator multiplies it by its own carrier f<sub>ci</sub>, giving DSB-SC.
A band-pass filter keeps one sideband and trims it to the channel's slot.
A linear summer adds all the channels into the composite FDM signal, which may itself modulate a radio carrier.

blocks.text: The receiver reverses this: a bank of band-pass filters separates the slots, each slot is coherently detected with its own carrier f<sub>ci</sub>, and a low-pass filter returns the voice. The carriers at both ends must agree closely, since an SSB frequency error moves every tone of the voice; telephone systems derived all carriers from one master oscillator.

Crosstalk, one channel heard in another, has three causes: filters with too little stop-band rejection, carriers that drift towards a neighbour, and nonlinearity in the summer or line amplifiers, whose intermodulation products fall into other slots. Wider guard bands, sharper crystal or ceramic filters, stable carriers and linear amplifiers are the cures.

sections.h3: The telephone hierarchy and other uses

blocks.text: Analog telephony built FDM in stages. A basic group puts 12 voice channels in 60 to 108 kHz: carriers at 64, 68, …, 108 kHz, lower sideband kept, so each channel owns a 4 kHz slot. The figure draws it with the band of each channel. Five groups make a supergroup of 60 channels in 312 to 552 kHz, and larger groupings followed for coaxial cable and microwave links.

The same idea is everywhere in radio. Broadcast stations are FDM with 9 kHz slots on medium wave. FM stereo multiplexes within one station: the sum L + R at 0 to 15 kHz, a 19 kHz pilot, and the difference L − R as DSB-SC on a 38 kHz subcarrier at 23 to 53 kHz (see FM stereo multiplexing and FM receivers). When each user of a shared medium owns a band, the access scheme is called FDMA. Time division multiplexing shares a channel in time instead, and OFDM overlaps orthogonal subcarriers with no guard bands (see the chapters Time division multiplexing, and OFDM and fading channels).

examples.question: Ten voice channels, each band-limited to 3.4 kHz, are frequency multiplexed with a 0.6 kHz guard band between adjacent channels. Find the total bandwidth with SSB and with DSB-SC, and the ratio.
steps: Ratio 73.4/39.4 = 1.86: the guard bands do not double, so DSB needs a little less than twice the band.
In the slot convention the answers would be 10 × (3.4 + 0.6) = 40 kHz and 10 × (6.8 + 0.6) = 74 kHz.
examples.answer: 39.4 kHz with SSB and 73.4 kHz with DSB-SC, a ratio of 1.86 (40 kHz and 74 kHz if each channel owns its guard band).

examples.question: In a basic group, carriers at 64, 68, …, 108 kHz carry 0.3 to 3.4 kHz voice channels as lower sidebands. Find the band of the channels on the 108 kHz and 104 kHz carriers, the gap between them and the band of the whole group.
steps: LSB of a carrier f<sub>ci</sub>: from f<sub>ci</sub> − 3.4 kHz to f<sub>ci</sub> − 0.3 kHz.
108 kHz carrier: 104.6 to 107.7 kHz. 104 kHz carrier: 100.6 to 103.7 kHz.
Gap: 104.6 − 103.7 = 0.9 kHz, which is the 4 kHz slot minus the 3.1 kHz of speech.
The lowest channel, on 64 kHz, occupies 60.6 to 63.7 kHz. The group spans 60 to 108 kHz: 12 × 4 = 48 kHz.
examples.answer: 104.6 to 107.7 kHz and 100.6 to 103.7 kHz, a 0.9 kHz gap; the group occupies 60 to 108 kHz (48 kHz).

traps: Multiplying N by the voice bandwidth alone. The guard bands must be added: 39.4 kHz, not 34 kHz, in the first example.
Saying DSB doubles the slot. Only the message part doubles: 7.1 kHz, not 8 kHz, for 3.1 kHz voice with 0.9 kHz guard bands.
Counting N guard bands when they sit only between channels. Ten channels have nine gaps.
Putting the FM stereo pilot at 38 kHz. The pilot is 19 kHz; 38 kHz is the suppressed subcarrier of L − R.

quiz.a: FDM sends several messages together by giving each a separate frequency band. A guard band is the unused strip between bands that lets filters separate them.

quiz.q: Why does voice FDM use SSB?
quiz.a: SSB needs W per channel against 2W for DSB, so nearly twice as many calls fit in the same band.

quiz.q: Three 3.1 kHz voice channels use 4 kHz slots starting at 100 kHz. Give the slots, the guard band and the total bandwidth.
quiz.a: Slots 100 to 104, 104 to 108 and 108 to 112 kHz; guard band 4 − 3.1 = 0.9 kHz; total 12 kHz.

quiz.q: Four 4 kHz channels are sent as DSB-SC on carriers of 100, 110, 120 and 130 kHz. Find the bands, the guard bands and the total bandwidth.
quiz.a: Bands 96 to 104, 106 to 114, 116 to 124 and 126 to 134 kHz; guard bands 2 kHz; total 134 − 96 = 38 kHz.

quiz.q: How many channels does a supergroup carry, and in what band?
quiz.a: Five groups of 12, so 60 channels, in 312 to 552 kHz (240 kHz).

quiz.q: Channel 2 of an FDM link carries faint speech from channel 1. Give two causes and a cure for each.
quiz.a: Too little filter rejection: sharper filters or wider guard bands. A drifting carrier: lock all carriers to one master oscillator. A nonlinear amplifier: reduce its level or use a more linear one.

quiz.q: Why must the summer and line amplifiers of an FDM system be linear?
quiz.a: A nonlinearity mixes channels and creates intermodulation products at sums and differences of their frequencies, which land in other slots as crosstalk that no receiver filter can remove.

beyond: Fibre networks use the same idea with light: wavelength-division multiplexing puts dozens of channels on separate wavelengths of one fibre. Cable TV and DOCSIS cable modems divide the coaxial band into FDM channels. Search next for DWDM, FDMA in satellite transponders and OFDMA.
